questions.q: Who is responsible for conducting fair elections in India?
questions.a: The Election Commission. A wrong answer suggests the student confuses the Election Commission with the government (legislature or executive), indicating they do not understand the need for an independent body to manage the fairness of the process.

questions.q: What does it mean when we say India has a system of "universal adult franchise"?
questions.a: It means every citizen who is 18 years or older has the right to vote, regardless of their wealth, caste, or religion. Answering incorrectly suggests the student thinks voting is reserved for certain groups or based on qualifications other than age, missing the core democratic value of equality.

questions.q: If a student thinks that the person standing next to them in the voting booth can see who they voted for, why is this incorrect?
questions.a: 1. Identify the concept of a "secret ballot." 2. Explain that the booth is designed for privacy. 3. Conclude that the system ensures no one knows your choice. A wrong answer shows a lack of understanding of how the system protects the voter from pressure.

questions.q: Why can't all 970 million citizens of India simply vote on every single law directly?
questions.a: It is physically and logistically impossible for 970 million people to debate and vote on every law daily. A wrong answer indicates the student hasn't grasped the necessity of "representative democracy" as a practical solution to governing large populations.

questions.q: Should a wealthy person have more votes than someone who is not wealthy? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, because democracy is based on equality; every adult gets one vote, no matter their wealth. A wrong answer suggests the student does not understand the principle of "one person, one vote," which is the foundation of our electoral system.

questions.q: Design a simple rule to ensure your class election for a picnic spot is "free and fair" like the Indian elections.
questions.a: A good answer would include: 1. A secret voting method (slips in a box), 2. An impartial teacher to count votes, 3. Everyone gets one vote. A poor answer ignores privacy or the impartiality of the person counting, failing to prevent "influence" or "cheating."
